CausalChain: HepG2 cells exhibit reduced mitochondrial number and altered metabolic profiles -> Mitochondrial dysfunction is known to impact Wnt/β-catenin signaling activity -> Aberrant Wnt/β-catenin activation supports enhanced cell survival and chemoresistance -> Thus, restoring mitochondrial function (via enhanced biogenesis or metabolic modulation) should normalize Wnt signaling -> Normalization of Wnt signaling is expected to re-sensitize cells to apoptotic cues and reduce tumorigenic potential
Hypothesis: Restoration of mitochondrial biogenesis or function in HepG2 cells will normalize Wnt/β-catenin signaling, thereby decreasing their chemoresistance and tumorigenic properties.
Abstract: HepG2 cells, originally classified as hepatocellular carcinoma but now widely recognized as a hepatoblastoma‐derived cell line, display distinct metabolic, genomic, and functional characteristics. Notably, their reduced mitochondrial content and attenuated expression of key drug‐metabolizing enzymes have been associated with altered signaling in pathways such as Wnt/β‐catenin. In this review-derived hypothesis, we propose that the metabolic state of HepG2 cells, particularly their mitochondrial dysfunction, serves as a pivotal regulator of aberrant Wnt signaling that underlies survival and chemoresistance. We hypothesize that restoration of mitochondrial function by enhancing biogenesis or activity will normalize Wnt/β‐catenin signaling, thereby reducing the tumorigenic and chemoresistant phenotypes of these cells. This model opens avenues to explore mitochondrial modulation as an adjuvant therapeutic strategy in liver cancer models represented by HepG2 cells.
